intervals.label: first beam and commissioning
intervals.note: Ends with the first proton-proton collisions; the same page states the LHC produced 'its first collisions on 23 November 2009'.
intervals.quote: The LHC circulated its first protons on 10 September 2008.

end.note: Run 1 ended in early 2013 with Long Shutdown 1; no CERN page fetched in this session gives the exact date, so year precision only.

intervals.label: Run 1
intervals.note: Start verified to the day; end is year-precision (see the end-date note). src:cern-lhc-prepares-new-achievements-2018 establishes that the second run covered 2015-2018, bounding Run 1's end before 2015.
intervals.quote: first high-energy collisions (7 TeV) on 30 March 2010

beam_energy.note: 3.5 TeV per beam in 2010-2011; the 2012 step to 4 TeV per beam is not stated on any CERN page fetched in this session.
beam_energy.quote: The first attempt for collisions at 7 TeV (3.5 TeV per beam) is scheduled for 30 March.

cms_energy.quote: first high-energy collisions (7 TeV) on 30 March 2010

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 1
intervals.note: Bounded by the sourced facts that Run 1 ended in early 2013 and that the second run began in 2015 ('It reached 13 TeV in 2015, at the start of its second run'). The CERN press release dating the final Run 1 beam extraction could not be re-fetched (home.cern returns 404 after its own redirect), so both bounds are year-precision.

intervals.label: Run 2
intervals.note: End date from src:cern-run2-conclusion-2018 ('On 3 December, the LHC's second run came to an end after three fantastic years') and the 3 December 2018 dateline of src:cern-lhc-prepares-new-achievements-2018.
intervals.quote: During this second run (2015-2018), the LHC performed beyond expectations

beam_energy.note: Half of the sourced 13 TeV centre-of-mass energy; no CERN page fetched in this session states 6.5 TeV per beam directly.

cms_energy.quote: It reached 13 TeV in 2015, at the start of its second run

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 2
intervals.note: Start = the 3 December 2018 dateline of the CERN article announcing LS2; end = the start of Run 3 physics collisions on 5 July 2022.
intervals.quote: With this second long shutdown starting now, we will prepare the machine for even more collisions at the design energy of 14 TeV.

intervals.label: Run 3
intervals.locator: home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3, news item dated 29 June 2026 ("So long and thanks for all the collisions!")
intervals.note: End = the day the last beams were dumped: "On Saturday 27 June at 6 am, the LHC’s Page 1 — the accelerator’s dashboard — said “goodbye” to collisions. The LHC operators dumped the last beams before the accelerator’s metamorphosis." (item dated 29 June 2026 on home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3). CERN’s farewell article of the same date: "Following its final physics run, the accelerator has been switched off to begin CERN’s Long Shutdown 3 (LS3)". So Run 3 ended in June 2026 as scheduled (the 29 January 2026 accelerator report gave the end of the LHC physics programme as 29 June 2026). Previously recorded at month precision (2026-06).
intervals.quote: A round of applause broke out in the CERN Control Centre on 5 July at 4.47 p.m. CEST when the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) detectors started recording high-energy collisions

beam_energy.quote: at the record collision energy of 13.6 trillion electronvolts (TeV) - 6.8 TeV per beam

cms_energy.quote: at the record collision energy of 13.6 trillion electronvolts (TeV) - 6.8 TeV per beam

end.note: The LHC itself restarts in mid-2030 (HiLumi LHC); the rest of the CERN complex restarts in stages from 2028 (see accelerator:ps, psb, sps, linac4).

intervals.label: Long Shutdown 3
intervals.locator: home.cern/science/long-shutdown-3, item of 5 August 2026 "The LHC is being warmed up from near absolute zero to room temperature"
intervals.note: LS3 installs the High-Luminosity LHC. Start = "The cryogenics team has been running the warm-up sequence since LS3 began on 29 June 2026." (CERN, 5 August 2026); the farewell article is also dated 29 June 2026. End is a schedule value, not a reported event: the same item says the stored helium is kept "ready to be used again once the accelerator resumes operation in mid-2030" and the 29 June 2026 article says the HiLumi LHC is "scheduled to begin operation in 2030". Corrected: this interval previously ended at a planned 2028, which is when the injector complex and other facilities start to restart ("from mid-2028 onwards" on the LS3 page), not the LHC.
intervals.quote: This phase, known as 'Long Shutdown 3' or 'LS3', is expected to last up to four years.

name: Large Hadron Collider
notes: Per-run beam energies are carried on the Interval.specs of each run (A3).
The 2012 increase from 3.5 to 4 TeV per beam is not stated on any CERN page fetched in this session; the Run 1 interval therefore records 3.5 TeV/beam with a note.
The LHC occupies the 26.7 km tunnel built for LEP (src:cern-lep-page: 'Its 27-kilometre tunnel now hosts the LHC').

beam_energy.note: Design beam energy. The energy actually delivered per run is on each run interval's specs; home.cern's key-figures table lists the current 'Nominal energy, protons: 6.8 TeV'.
beam_energy.quote: The bypass diodes - the electrical components that protect the magnets in case of quench - will be shielded, as a prerequisite for extending the LHC beam energy to 7 TeV after the LS2

cms_energy.locator: arXiv:2305.16623 (JINST 19 (2024) P05063), abstract on the first page of the PDF
cms_energy.note: Design centre-of-mass energy; home.cern (2018) repeats 'the design energy of 14 TeV'. Highest energy actually reached is 13.6 TeV (Run 3).
cms_energy.quote: It was originally designed for proton-proton collisions at a centre-of √ mass energy of 𝑠 = 14 TeV with an instantaneous luminosity of L = 1034 cm−2 s−1

peak_luminosity.note: Routinely achieved start-of-fill luminosity in Run 2; the design value is 1e34 cm^-2 s^-1 (2008 JINST 3 S08003, chapter 1).
peak_luminosity.quote: During Run 2 of the LHC, a luminosity of $\mathcal{L}=2\times 10^{34}\mathrm{cm}^{-2}\mathrm{s}^{-1}$ was routinely achieved at the start of fills, twice the design luminosity.

summary.plain: The world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator: a 27-kilometre ring of superconducting magnets under the Swiss-French border that steers two beams of protons in opposite directions and smashes them together inside four large experiments, including ATLAS.
summary.technical: Superconducting proton-proton (and heavy-ion) collider of 26 659 m circumference in the former LEP tunnel; 1232 main dipoles at 1.9 K; design 7 TeV/beam (14 TeV cms) at 1e34 cm^-2 s^-1; ran at 3.5-4 TeV/beam in Run 1, 6.5 TeV/beam in Run 2 and 6.8 TeV/beam in Run 3.
